Robert R. Moton, who led the plantation songs at Hampton for nearly twenty years, wrote in 1909 that once students had caught the air, the best results usually came from letting them sing "as seems to them most easy and natural".

source.en: Religious Folk Songs of the Negro, New Edition (Hampton, Va., 1909), "Note to New Edition", p. vi; reprinted in Dett's 1927 edition

The songbook's editor, R. Nathaniel Dett, wrote that its tunes and harmonies were set down as the students sang them, in a tradition of singing these songs going back to 1868.

source.en: R. Nathaniel Dett, ed., Religious Folk-Songs of the Negro as Sung at Hampton Institute (1927), introduction, section IX, p. xviii
